note: Runtime layer registry. `source` blocks are read by scripts/build-layers.mjs in CI; the browser ignores them.

groups.label: Regulatory floodplains
groups.blurb: New York City has had two simultaneously-operative, mutually inconsistent regulatory floodplains for over a decade. Turn both on.

groups.label: Future floodplains & sea level rise
groups.blurb: Projections, not forecasts. Every one of these carries a scenario and a horizon — read the labels before you read the map.

groups.label: What the water actually did
groups.blurb: Sandy, Ida, and the sensors watching for the next one.

groups.label: Rainfall & stormwater
groups.blurb: The flooding FEMA's product does not describe.

groups.label: The waterfront edge
groups.blurb: Where the city meets the water, who may stand there, and what holds it in place.

groups.label: The harbour as worked space
groups.blurb: Charted by the navy, dredged by the Army, and largely absent from the municipal commons.

layers.label: Hurricane Evacuation Zones
layers.notes: Six zones, version 26b, revised quarterly. An administrative geography — it tells you who is told to leave, not where water goes. Pair it with the SLOSH inundation layer underneath.

layers.label: FloodNet street sensors
layers.notes: 479 live street sensors. CUNY co-leads this. The events table (aq7i-eu5q) has no geometry — join on sensor_id.

layers.label: Sandy Inundation Zone (2012)
layers.notes: Field-verified through February 2013. Historical — it will never update. Where the water actually went, against three maps that each claim to say where it would go.

layers.label: 2015 Preliminary FIRM
layers.notes: The floodplain the NYC Building Code requires for new and substantially improved buildings. FEMA agreed in October 2016 that its models overstated flood elevations by 1 to 2.5 ft citywide, and committed to reissue. No revised maps have been adopted.

layers.label: 2007 Effective FIRM
layers.notes: The floodplain flood insurance rates actually run off. Simultaneously operative with the 2015 Preliminary FIRM, and inconsistent with it.

layers.label: NYC Stormwater Flood Maps
layers.scenarioNote: This is the Ida layer — the pluvial one. Map Ida's deaths and basement flooding against the FEMA floodplain and there is almost no overlap. That is the finding, not an error: FEMA's product is coastal.

layers.label: NYS Sea Level Rise & Future Floodplain Extent
layers.scenarioNote: 32 floodplains: 8 sea-level-rise increments against 4 annual-chance events. No licence is stated anywhere for this dataset — confirm with NYSERDA before re-serving publicly.
layers.license: NONE STATED — verify before public re-serving

layers.label: Hurricane inundation (SLOSH) by evacuation zone
layers.notes: The National Hurricane Center's 2020 SLOSH model, NE1 basin, 10 m, surge at high tide. The physical layer under the administrative one.

layers.label: Flood Vulnerability Index
layers.notes: By census tract. fshri is 12 socioeconomic indicators; ss_* is storm surge and tid_* is tidal, each for current / 2050s / 2080s. Every field ships as text — cast before you compare.

layers.label: Historically redlined areas (HOLC)
layers.notes: Put this under the floodplain and over the environmental justice areas. Three layers, one publisher.

layers.label: NYS Disadvantaged Communities (2023)
layers.notes: Census tract, statewide. Carries coastal_flooding_storm_risk, inland_flooding_risk, days_above_90_degrees_2050 and low_vegetative_cover as attributes.

layers.label: Waterfront Public Access Areas
layers.notes: Privately owned, publicly accessible. 38 columns including Chair Certification and CPC Approval dates — the paperwork trail of a right of way.

layers.label: Human-powered boat launches
layers.notes: Sixty-three places a person may put a kayak in the water. One of the two best ethnographic hooks in the survey.

layers.label: Saltwater fishing sites
layers.notes: 107 points, with an Ownership field. Who fishes where, and on whose land, is a question a map can pose and only fieldwork can answer.

layers.label: Planimetric shoreline
layers.notes: Use this one for drawing. For analysis use the tidally coordinated shoreline instead.

layers.label: Tidally coordinated shoreline
layers.notes: Coordinated against Kings Point, Bergen West, Sandy Hook and The Battery. Use this one for analysis. 24.5 MB.

layers.label: Waterfront Revitalization Program boundary
layers.notes: Use the live service, not the 2015 shapefile cbn4-bn4p.

layers.label: Landward coastal area boundary
layers.notes: The line that legally defines “the coastal zone”.

layers.label: NY Rising community reconstruction areas
layers.notes: In New York City these were digitised from neighbourhoods and business recovery zones, then adjusted by Community Planning Committees using damage assessments. An administratively drawn neighbourhood boundary, produced by committee in response to a flood, still marked preliminary.

layers.label: NYC wetlands
layers.notes: Explicitly carries no jurisdictional authority. For regulatory wetlands go to NYSDEC — and read what DEC says about its own maps.

layers.label: Waterfront parks
layers.notes: Filtered to WATERFRONT = true from Parks Properties. This is how you get Brooklyn Bridge Park, the East River Esplanade and Freshkills — there are no separate layers for them.

layers.label: DEC regulatory tidal wetlands
layers.notes: Layer 1, not 0. Troy Dam to the tip of Staten Island. NYSDEC forbids secondary distribution and requires credit — built here, held back from public re-serving until DEC's position is in writing.

layers.label: DEC coastal erosion hazard areas
layers.notes: DEC says explicitly this is “an initial screening tool only” and that the legal boundaries are the paper maps filed with municipalities. A good teaching point about the gap between a shapefile and a regulation.

layers.label: DEC remediation parcels (brownfields)
layers.notes: Updated nightly. Intersect with the floodplain for the toxic-sites-in-the-flood-zone exercise. Small; tiles beautifully.

layers.label: USACE navigation channels
layers.notes: Ambrose, Anchorage, Kill Van Kull, Arthur Kill. The harbour as a maintained industrial surface.

layers.label: USACE eHydro survey footprints
layers.notes: 779 dated channel-survey footprints. A record of when somebody last measured the bottom.

layers.label: Shoreline construction (NOAA chart)
layers.notes: Piers, wharves, bulkheads, seawalls. The City publishes no dataset of the structures holding its own shoreline in place — for ~520 miles of edge, everything usable comes from the navy's chartmakers. Rebuilt every Saturday night.

layers.label: Pilings (NOAA chart)
layers.notes: 1,667 pilings — the ghosts of piers that are otherwise gone from every map the city keeps.

layers.label: Green infrastructure assets
layers.notes: Carries Asset_Type, Status, Sewer_Type, Outfall, receiving waterbody and Constructed_Date. One of the few city layers rich enough to ask when as well as where.

layers.label: Catch basins
layers.notes: 154,212 points and no condition field. A density layer, not a maintenance layer — which is itself the point when you put it beside 44,593 “catch basin clogged” complaints.

layers.label: MS4 outfalls
layers.notes: With catch basins, the only sewer geometry the City releases. There is no CSO outfall layer, no sewer mains, no regulators, no interceptors.

parked_note: Nothing parked yet. Parking a layer is moving one entry from `layers` into `parked` — the app reads only `layers`.
